newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Milosevic scolds Bosnian Serb leader over feud.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic scolds Bosnian Serb leader over feud.

text.p: Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic warned Bosnian Serb leader Biljana Plavsic on Wednesday that her power struggle with hardline nationalists was dangerous and could divide Serb territory.
Milosevic, patron of the Bosnian Serbs, scolded Plavsic after she rejected his offer to mediate in her confrontation with hardliners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.

The Serbian leader said that the struggle threatened to divide Bosnia's Serb Republic between Plavsic supporters in the northwestern town of Banja Luka and Karadzic loyalists to the east based in Pale, outside Sarajevo.

"Alignment with either Pale or Banja Luka could bring the Serb Republic into great danger and jeopardise the vital interests of both the people and the republic," Milosevic said, quoted by the state Tanjug news agency.
"In these difficult times politicians are expected not to defend their pride but the interests of the people," he added.
Diplomats say the Serbian leader has rebuilt links with Karadzic and his allies since he forced them to sign the Dayton peace agreement against their will in 1995.

Karadzic, accused of crimes against humanity by a U.N. tribunal, has travelled to Belgrade more than once this year to hold talks with Milosevic, who has often relished the role of kingmaker among Bosnian Serbs.
Plavsic and Karadzic allies have been locked in a power struggle for more than a week since she accused them of large-scale corruption.
Plavsic's aides said on Tuesday evening she had "nothing to discuss" with Milosevic, who armed and directed the Bosnian Serbs for more than three years of war.
Her rival, Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's multi-ethnic collective presidency, accepted the invitation to meet Milosevic in Belgrade, the capital of Serbian-led Yugoslavia.

Plavsic dissolved parliament last week and called for new elections on September 1. Hardliners dismissed her decision and held a session of assembly anyway, rewriting laws to enable her recall and to strip her of defence powers.
Diplomats are concerned two competing authorities in Serb territory could emerge, one in the west and one directed by Karadzic in the east.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, reiterating a message from NATO countries, said on Wednesday in Madrid that his government believed Plavsic had acted in line with the constitution when she dissolved the Bosnian Serb assembly.
But it was not clear how Western powers would react if Karadzic's ruling party managed to win a favourable ruling from the Serb constitutional court.
Plavsic's campaign against corruption has struck a chord among many ordinary Serbs, who live in abject poverty. Serb authorities have not paid out pensions or salaries to public employees for months.
Supporters of Plavsic staged a rally in Prijedor, near Banja Luka, on Tuesday and planned to hold another rally in Bijeljina to show she enjoyed sympathy in the east.
"At the moment we are living in a situation where part of the people are sucking the blood of the rest of the people like leeches," Plavsic said at the Prijedor rally.
"They are not paying customs, they are not paying taxes, they are robbing the state," she said.
Karadzic's effort to crush Plavsic has focused attention on his persistent influence and the failure of major powers to arrest him and other indicted war criminals.
The former Sarajevo psychiatrist was forced out of public office last year under international pressure when he promised to stay out of politics.
